userStories.title: Make Stripe webhook processing idempotent
userStories.description: The Stripe webhook handler processes every delivery unconditionally, with no record of which event IDs it has already applied. Stripe guarantees at-least-once delivery and retries any non-2xx response, so a duplicate or retried delivery re-applies its side effects. This matters most where the handler is not naturally idempotent: granting entitlements for one-time purchases (lifetime access, tax packages) and appending payment history rows. It also matters after the signature-verification fix in this branch, because Stripe will now redeliver the backlog of events that previously failed with 400, potentially replaying months of accumulated events in a burst.
acceptanceCriteria: A stripe_webhook_events table exists via a Supabase migration, keyed on the Stripe event id as primary key, with a received_at timestamp
functions/api/stripe-webhook.ts records each event id before dispatching to a handler, and skips dispatch when the id is already present
The insert-and-check is a single atomic operation so two concurrent deliveries of the same event cannot both proceed
An already-processed event returns 200 so Stripe stops retrying it
A delivery that fails mid-handler does not leave the event marked processed, so Stripe's retry can still apply it
One-time purchase handlers (lifetime, tax packages) are verified to grant entitlement exactly once under duplicate delivery
A retention policy or index is in place so the table does not grow unbounded
userStories.notes: Found during the iteration-5 audit of functions/api/stripe-webhook.ts, alongside the constructEventAsync signature bug fixed in commit 276f5a9. Deliberately NOT bundled with that fix: this needs a database migration plus handler restructuring, which is more than one iteration of work. Sequence matters - the signature fix means events now actually reach the handlers, so idempotency should land before the endpoint is re-enabled in the Stripe dashboard and the retry backlog is replayed.

userStories.title: Authenticate and rate limit /api/send-email
userStories.description: functions/api/send-email.ts performs no authentication. Any client can POST a recipient, subject and up to 100 KB of HTML and have it delivered through our SMTP credentials and domain. The sender-spoofing half of this was fixed by pinning the sender to configuration, but an unauthenticated caller can still send mail that genuinely originates from us, to any address, with any content. CORS does not mitigate this - it constrains browsers, not curl. The only limit today is the generic 100 requests/minute default tier in functions/api/_middleware.ts, and because RATE_LIMIT_KV is not bound in wrangler.toml that limit falls back to an in-memory Map which is per-isolate and therefore close to unenforced across Cloudflare's edge.
acceptanceCriteria: POST /api/send-email without valid credentials returns 401 and sends no mail
Browser callers (email.ts, invoicing.ts, transactionEmails.ts, supportTickets.ts) attach the Supabase session JWT, and the endpoint verifies it
The verified caller identity, not the request body, determines the recipient wherever the mail is addressed to the user themselves

Any flow that must send before a session exists (e.g. newsletter welcome) is identified and given an explicit design - either a server-side trigger or a scoped single-use token - rather than being left open
send-email is given its own strict rate limit tier in functions/api/_middleware.ts rather than the shared 100/min default
A KV namespace is created and bound as RATE_LIMIT_KV in wrangler.toml so rate limits are enforced across isolates rather than per-instance
An abuse test confirms an unauthenticated caller cannot send, and an authenticated caller cannot exceed the new limit
userStories.notes: SECURITY - HIGH. Found during the iteration-7 audit. The sender-spoofing vector was closed separately by pinning the sender server-side, which was safe to do immediately because no caller ever set a from address. Authentication was NOT bundled with it because it requires changing four browser call sites to attach a session token AND a product decision about flows that legitimately send before a user is signed in - notably sendNewsletterWelcomeEmail. Requiring auth without resolving that would silently break newsletter signup. Related: the in-memory rate limiter in functions/api/_middleware.ts is a stated fallback, but with no KV binding it is the ONLY path, and its own comment understates the impact - Workers isolates are per-colo and short-lived, so counters reset constantly.

userStories.title: Authenticate /api/claude and attribute AI spend per user
userStories.description: functions/api/claude.ts performs no authentication. Anyone who finds the URL can use our Anthropic API key as a general-purpose LLM proxy: they control the full message list, the system prompt, and the sampling parameters, and the cost lands on our bill. Per-request cost is now bounded (model restricted to known aliases, maxTokens clamped, prompt sizes capped), but request volume is not: the endpoint falls under the generic 100/min default tier in functions/api/_middleware.ts, which with RATE_LIMIT_KV unbound degrades to a per-isolate in-memory Map. There is also no record of who spent what - the response carries Anthropic's usage object but nothing is persisted, so there is no way to attribute cost, detect abuse, or enforce per-tier AI quotas.

userStories.notes: SECURITY / COST - HIGH. Found during the iteration-8 audit. userStories.title: Model Monte Carlo returns log-normally instead of additively
userStories.description: runMonteCarloSimulation draws a normal monthly return and applies it as value * (1 + r). A normal draw is unbounded below, so at high volatility inputs - and 60-120% annual volatility is ordinary for crypto, which is what this tool projects - a single month can return worse than -100% and drive the simulated portfolio value negative. A negative balance then compounds, so the affected paths are not merely pessimistic but meaningless, and they contaminate the percentile bands, the average return and the probability-of-profit figure that sit beside the drawdown metric. Real prices cannot go below zero; the standard treatment is geometric Brownian motion, where the log return is normal and the price factor exp(r) is always positive.
acceptanceCriteria: Simulated portfolio value never goes negative for any volatility input
Monthly growth is drawn as a log-normal factor, with the drift term corrected for volatility drag so the mean annual return still matches the caller's expectedReturn
At low volatility the percentile bands stay close to the current output, so the change is visibly a refinement rather than a different tool
probabilityOfProfit and the percentile bands are re-checked at 60% and 120% volatility and no longer include impossible paths
The 100% cap on drawdown becomes unreachable in practice rather than load-bearing
The same review is applied to the volatility and Sharpe figures in compareMultipleAssets, which use the same additive assumption
userStories.notes: Found during the iteration-14 audit while fixing the max-drawdown metric, which was returning a hardcoded-zero result (commit on branch claude/lucid-goodall-mi34c1). Deliberately not bundled: switching the return model changes every number this premium feature outputs - percentiles, expected return, probability of profit - so it wants its own change with before/after comparison at several volatility levels, not a quiet edit inside a bug fix. The drawdown metric is capped at 100% in the meantime so the displayed figure stays well-formed; that cap is a symptom of this issue and should become redundant once the model is corrected.

userStories.title: Review whether the wash sale rule should apply to crypto at all
userStories.description: calculateWashSaleImpact in taxCalculator.ts applies the 30-day wash sale rule to cryptocurrency disposals. The wash sale rule in IRC section 1091 is written for 'stock or securities', and the IRS treats cryptocurrency as property rather than a security, so the rule has generally not applied to crypto. If that is right, the calculator tells users a loss is disallowed when it is claimable, which would lead them to delay a repurchase for 30 days or forgo a deduction they are entitled to - the calculator causing the harm it exists to prevent. This needs a position taken by someone qualified rather than a code change made on assumption: proposals to extend the rule to digital assets have recurred in Congress, so the answer may also be time-dependent and may differ for tokens held in ways that look more like securities.
acceptanceCriteria: A documented position on whether section 1091 applies to the assets this platform covers, with a date and source
If the rule does not apply, calculateWashSaleImpact either says so plainly or is removed rather than silently reporting a disallowed loss
If the position is that it may apply in future, the wording distinguishes current treatment from proposed legislation
findTaxLossHarvestingOpportunities is checked for the same assumption, since its whole premise is harvesting losses
Any user-facing wording is reviewed against the existing 'estimate only, consult a tax professional' disclaimer
userStories.notes: Found during the iteration-15 audit. Deliberately NOT changed in code: unlike the arithmetic defects fixed in this branch, this is a question of tax law rather than a bug with a demonstrably correct answer, and it is exactly the kind of call that should be made by a qualified professional and recorded, not inferred by an agent from a code comment. Flagging it as a question, not a defect. Also note that the assumed harvesting tax rates in findTaxLossHarvestingOpportunities are hardcoded to 22% short-term and 15% long-term regardless of the filer's actual bracket, which is worth revisiting in the same pass.

userStories.title: Back the backtesting tool with live historical prices instead of a bundled snapshot table
userStories.description: src/services/backtesting.ts ships a hardcoded HISTORICAL_PRICES table of roughly 20 quarterly snapshots per asset, ending 2024-12-09 for all three supported assets. Because the table is static, its coverage decays: every day that passes moves more of the tool's advertised periods outside the data. As of this iteration the '1 Year' preset has no data at all, and the '2 Years' preset covers only its first three months. The immediate correctness and honesty problems are fixed in this iteration (windows are clamped to actual coverage, the clamp is disclosed in the UI, unavailable presets are disabled, prices between snapshots are interpolated instead of snapped to the nearest anchor), but the underlying fix is to fetch real daily history. The platform already integrates CoinGecko (src/services/coingecko.ts), whose market_chart/range endpoint returns daily OHLC history, so the data source exists - the work is caching, rate limiting, error and offline fallback, and widening the supported asset list, which is more than one iteration.

userStories.title: Consolidate the two parallel technical-indicator implementations
userStories.description: The platform carries two independent technical-analysis engines. src/services/tradingIndicators.ts (474 lines) backs the /trading-indicators page. src/services/technicalIndicators.ts (687 lines) implements the same indicators again - SMA, EMA, RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands, Stochastic, ATR - plus a richer generateTechnicalSignals, and feeds src/components/TechnicalIndicators.tsx, which is imported by nothing: a grep for the component name across src returns only its own definition. userStories.title: Move 2FA verification server-side and stop storing TOTP secrets in readable plaintext
userStories.description: Two-factor verification runs entirely in the browser. signInWithTwoFactor reads two_factor_secret out of public.users into client JavaScript and compares the code there, and the secret and all recovery codes are stored in plaintext columns. The RLS fix in this iteration stops other users reading those columns, but the owner's own browser still receives them on every login, so a second factor is only as strong as the client executing the check: anything with the session token can read the secret and generate codes indefinitely, and the check itself can simply be skipped. There is also no per-account attempt limiting on the code itself - the login rate limiter is keyed on email in module memory (src/services/auth.ts), so it resets on reload and is per-tab, leaving a six-digit code with a +/-1 step window brute-forceable. Verification belongs behind an endpoint that holds the secret encrypted at rest, counts attempts server-side, and rejects a code already spent in its time step.
acceptanceCriteria: TOTP verification happens server-side; the secret never reaches the browser after enrollment
two_factor_secret is encrypted at rest, and recovery codes are stored hashed rather than in plaintext so a database read cannot replay them
Failed 2FA attempts are counted server-side per account and lock out after a threshold, surviving a page reload
A TOTP code cannot be replayed within its own time step (last-used counter recorded per account)
The pending-2FA session gate is either kept or replaced by a server-issued pre-auth token that cannot act as a full session
Supabase's own MFA support is evaluated first, since adopting it would remove most of this code rather than reimplement it
userStories.notes: Opened during iteration 3 alongside the RLS fix for admins_select_all_users. Deliberately out of scope for that fix: the RLS hole was a one-line predicate error with a demonstrable exploit and a safe correction, whereas this is a design change spanning an edge function, a schema migration with a backfill for existing enrolled users, and a re-enrollment story for secrets that cannot be migrated - more than one iteration. Note the currently-unused verifyTwoFactorCode and redeemRecoveryCode in src/services/twoFactor.ts should be folded into whatever server-side path replaces this, not left as a second client-side copy.

userStories.title: Persist the transaction ledger for saved portfolios instead of storing only a position
userStories.description: The holdings table stores a position - amount and average_buy_price - and no transaction history, so getPortfolio loads every saved holding with an empty transactions array. Cost basis is now derived by replaying the ledger (recalculateHoldingFromTransactions), and this iteration bridges the gap by synthesising a single opening transfer_in from the stored amount and average price. That keeps the arithmetic correct going forward but loses the real history: a user who logs in cannot see the trades behind a position, the holding-period split that the tax report depends on cannot be reconstructed, and any future change of accounting method (FIFO or specific identification rather than average cost) has nothing to recompute from. Transactions need their own table with RLS, a writer on every mutation path, and a backfill that turns each existing holding's opening balance into a real row.
acceptanceCriteria: A transactions table exists with RLS scoped to the owning portfolio, and holdings link to it
addHolding, removeFromHolding, addStakingReward and addTransaction persist their transaction rather than only mutating the in-memory holding
getPortfolio loads real transactions; the synthesised opening transfer_in is removed once a holding has genuine history
A migration backfills one opening row per existing holding so no saved position loses its basis
The tax report and holding-period logic read from the persisted ledger instead of the position snapshot
Accounting method is stated in one place, so FIFO or specific identification can be added without a second basis implementation
userStories.notes: Opened during iteration 4 while consolidating four divergent copies of the cost-basis maths. Deliberately out of scope for that fix: a schema migration plus backfill plus rewriting the read path is more than one iteration, and the arithmetic errors needed fixing whether or not the history is persisted. Note the synthesised opening transfer_in is load-bearing until this lands - removing it without persisting real transactions would make the ledger replay zero out every saved holding.

userStories.title: Give the scheduled endpoints their own secret instead of authenticating with the Supabase service role key
userStories.description: check-price-alerts and send-newsletter authenticate the scheduled worker by comparing the Authorization header against SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY. That key is the database god-key: it bypasses every RLS policy on every table. Using it as an HTTP bearer token means it is transmitted to a Pages Function on every cron run and sits in the request headers of any log line, error report or trace that captures them, and the workers hold it in their own environment purely to present it. A leak is total database compromise rather than the ability to trigger a newsletter early. These endpoints need a dedicated shared secret with no database authority, rotatable without touching Supabase, so that the blast radius of the credential matches what it actually authorises.
acceptanceCriteria: A dedicated secret (e.g. CRON_SHARED_SECRET) authenticates the scheduled endpoints; SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY is no longer used as a bearer token
The workers in workers/ send the new secret and no longer need the service role key in their environment unless they query the database directly
Rotation is documented, and the endpoints accept a previous value during a rotation window so a rotation does not drop a cron run
Deployment docs and wrangler-cron.toml / wrangler-newsletter.toml comments name the new secret
isAuthorizedScheduledRequest keeps failing closed when the secret is unset
userStories.notes: Opened during iteration 5 while removing the X-Cloudflare-Cron auth bypass from both endpoints. Deliberately out of scope for that fix: the bypass was a one-line predicate with a demonstrable exploit, whereas swapping the credential needs a new secret provisioned in the Cloudflare dashboard for Pages and both workers, plus a rotation window, and cannot be verified from the repo alone. Note the endpoints still need the service role key for their own Supabase queries - only its use as the bearer token should change.

userStories.title: Exchange API credentials are encrypted with a key derived only from the public user id
userStories.description: encryptCredentials in src/services/exchangeConnections.ts runs AES-256-GCM with a key derived by PBKDF2 from `userId + ':credentials-encryption-salt-v1'` and a hardcoded salt. Every input is either public or in the source, and userId is stored in the same row as the ciphertext, so anyone who can read exchange_connections can derive the key and decrypt every stored exchange API key and secret. There is no secret in the key derivation at all - this is obfuscation with the shape of encryption, and the 100,000 PBKDF2 iterations buy nothing when the password is known. A database dump, a backup, a leaked service role key, or an RLS mistake of the kind found in US-108 turns directly into exchange credentials. The fix is to encrypt server-side with a key the browser never sees, held as a Cloudflare secret or in a KMS, behind an endpoint that decrypts only for the authenticated owner.
acceptanceCriteria: Encryption and decryption happen server-side with a key that is never sent to the browser
The key comes from a managed secret (Cloudflare secret binding or KMS), not from any value stored beside the ciphertext
Stored ciphertext is versioned so existing rows can be re-encrypted, with a documented migration for anything already saved
Decrypted credentials are returned only to the authenticated owner and never logged
The UI states plainly what protection is and is not in place, and continues to steer users to read-only exchange keys
The misleading 'AES-256-GCM' framing in the code comments is corrected so the next reader is not reassured by it
userStories.notes: Found during iteration 6. NOT exploitable in production today: src/components/ExchangeConnections.tsx is imported by nothing - grep for the component name across src returns only its own definition - so no user can currently enter real exchange credentials through the UI. That is the only reason this is filed rather than fixed immediately, and it is also the reason it MUST be fixed before the component is ever mounted. Treat mounting ExchangeConnections as blocked on this story. Same unmounted-component situation as US-107.

userStories.title: Make sign-out-all-devices revoke the Supabase session, not just the application's own marker
userStories.description: Session tracking in src/services/sessionManager.ts is advisory. invalidateAllSessions deletes rows from user_sessions, and isSessionValid consults that table, but the Supabase refresh token on the other device is untouched and stays valid. After the PGRST116 fix in this iteration a revoked device does get signed out - but only because the application chooses to sign itself out on the next validity check. Anything holding the refresh token that does not run that check, such as a direct call to the Supabase REST API or a modified client, keeps full access with the user's RLS permissions. The session timeout has the same shape: it is enforced from a localStorage timestamp the user controls, so editing bi_last_activity extends a session indefinitely. Genuine revocation needs the auth server to invalidate the refresh token, via supabase.auth.admin.signOut from a privileged endpoint.
acceptanceCriteria: Signing out all devices revokes refresh tokens through the Supabase auth admin API, so other devices cannot refresh
Terminating a single session from the device list revokes that session's token rather than only deleting the tracking row
The privileged call happens server-side; the service role key is never exposed to the browser
Session expiry is enforced against a server-side timestamp rather than a client-writable localStorage value
isSessionValid keeps failing closed on a definitively absent session row and open only on a genuinely missing table
The UI does not claim other devices are signed out until the revocation has actually succeeded
userStories.notes: Opened during iteration 7 while fixing the PGRST116 misclassification that made remote revocation a no-op. Deliberately out of scope for that fix: revoking refresh tokens needs a new privileged endpoint holding the service role key plus a change to how expiry is measured, whereas the misclassification was a one-line error-code confusion with a definite correct answer. Note the two fixes compound - without this story, revocation is honoured only by a cooperating client.

userStories.title: Decide the fate of the 24 unreferenced components and the services behind them
userStories.description: Twenty-four of the roughly forty-five components in src/components are imported by nothing: AILearningAssistant, AMASessions, AdUnit, ApiAccess, Certifications, CustomDashboard, EarlyAccess, EmptyState, EnrollmentPrompt, ErrorStates, ExchangeConnections, FormElements, GEOContent, InteractiveCourses, OptimizedImage, PortfolioShareModal, QAForum, ResearchReports, RiskAssessmentQuiz, SuccessStories, SupportTicketForm, TechnicalIndicators, TransactionImport and VideoLibrary. Most have a backing service in src/services and, in several cases, tables and RLS policies in supabase/migrations, so the repository carries a substantial amount of machinery for features no user can reach. Because nothing imports them they are tree-shaken out of the build, so this is not shipped weight - it is maintenance burden and, more seriously, a source of false assurance: work has already been spent auditing and fixing code in this set (US-107 on duplicated indicator maths, US-111 on exchange credential encryption) that could equally have been spent on live code, and a reader cannot tell reachable code from unreachable without grepping. Each one needs a decision: mount it, or delete it with its service and migrations.
acceptanceCriteria: Every component in the list is either mounted on a route or deleted
Deleting a component also removes its service, types and any tables or policies that exist only for it
Anything mounted rather than deleted is reviewed first - several carry known defects (US-107, US-111) that must not reach users
A check that fails on a component with no importer runs in CI, so the set cannot silently grow again
The decision for each is recorded, so a component deliberately kept for imminent use is distinguishable from one that was forgotten
userStories.notes: Found during iteration 8 after two iterations were partly spent on code that turned out to be unreachable. Deliberately not done as a single change: deleting twenty-four components with their services and migrations is a large, irreversible sweep needing per-feature judgement about intent, and mounting any of them is a product decision rather than a fix. Until this is resolved, CHECK THAT A COMPONENT IS MOUNTED BEFORE INVESTING IN IT. The reverse also applies - US-111 must be resolved before ExchangeConnections is ever mounted.

userStories.title: Enforce premium entitlements server-side rather than in the browser
userStories.description: Every paywall on the platform is a client-side branch. The gates in src/services/subscriptionLimits.ts read subscription_status and subscription_expires_at from the user's own profile row and decide in the browser whether to render a premium feature, and the premium features themselves are computed client-side from public data. Anyone can edit the returned profile object, or simply call the underlying service function from the console, and obtain the paid feature. The expiry checks corrected in this iteration make the gates internally consistent, but consistency is not enforcement: nothing on the server declines to serve a premium result to a free account. Features whose value comes from server work - AI portfolio analysis via /api/claude, premium exports, research reports, tax packages - need the entitlement checked where the work happens, and the row users can read should not be the sole source of truth for what they have paid for.
acceptanceCriteria: Server-side endpoints that perform paid work verify the caller's entitlement before doing it, from the database rather than from anything the client sends
The entitlement check reads subscription_status together with subscription_expires_at, matching the client-side rule, so the two cannot diverge
RLS prevents a user from writing their own subscription_status or subscription_expires_at; only the Stripe webhook path may set them
Client-side gates remain, as UX rather than as security, and are documented as such so nobody mistakes them for enforcement

userStories.title: Audit the remaining unconditional write policies and the grants behind them
userStories.description: A sweep of all 128 tables found RLS enabled everywhere and one table with no policy at all (sponsored_disclosures, which therefore denies everything and fails closed). It also found nine write-capable policies with an unconditional predicate. Two were dangerous and are fixed in this iteration: tax_report_purchases and scam_reporter_reputation both carried FOR ALL USING (true). The remaining seven are INSERT-only policies on tables that genuinely accept anonymous writes - certificate_views, share_views, research_subscribers, wallet_auth_nonces, newsletter_subscribers (twice) and affiliate_clicks. Those are intentional public endpoints, but none of them is rate limited or deduplicated at the database level, so anyone can inflate view counts, stuff the newsletter list, fabricate affiliate click attribution, or fill wallet_auth_nonces without bound. Each needs a decision: constrain the insert (a CHECK on shape, a uniqueness constraint, a per-IP or per-window limit), or accept the write and document why. sponsored_disclosures needs a policy or removal, since a table that denies every caller is either dead or broken.

userStories.notes: Opened during iteration 12 alongside the tax_report_purchases and scam_reporter_reputation fixes. userStories.description: Calendar dates that a user sees or enters now use their local timezone (toLocalISODate / todayLocalISODate in src/lib/utils.ts), and stored date-only values are parsed as local rather than UTC midnight.
